radians"] ["question-9284b07a-9db4-5c4c-b135-110855ca0f14" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta $ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $100$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
100=2r+r\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that

$$
\theta =\frac{100-2r}{r}=\frac{100}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{100}{r}-2) \\  & =50r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A$, so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=50-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 50-2r & =0 \\ r & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=25$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(25)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(25)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=25$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Finally, when $r=25$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\frac{100}{r}-2 \\  & =\frac{100}{25}-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9284b07a-9db4-5c4c-b135-110855ca0f14" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579" :answer-field/id #uuid "f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579"] ["answer-fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b" :answer/id #uuid "fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b"] ["answer-fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b" :answer/value "2"] ["answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579" :answer-field/correct "answer-fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b"] ["answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579" :answer-field/choices "answer-fe0f3a0e-95e4-5ef5-9aec-3c4c7af2e50b"] ["question-9284b07a-9db4-5c4c-b135-110855ca0f14" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-f6880c81-e1e8-5f43-89ee-3d61afafa579"] [17592186100836 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9284b07a-9db4-5c4c-b135-110855ca0f14"] ["question-06dbc133-9492-57ef-8ac9-643d61a66e1b" :question/id #uuid "06dbc133-9492-57ef-8ac9-643d61a66e1b"] ["question-06dbc133-9492-57ef-8ac9-643d61a66e1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-344853"] ["question-06dbc133-9492-57ef-8ac9-643d61a66e1b" :question/problem "![](images/9e/9ea7b23d8dd14a0ed092152592800022400ee73e7b371146f5e972900f2c2f29.png)

$\text{m}$"] ["question-06dbc133-9492-57ef-8ac9-643d61a66e1b" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ be the radius of the semicircles (the same for both semicircles) and let $x$ be the length of the other side of the rectangle. We want to maximize the area

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2rx.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2r(60-\pi r) \\  & =120r-2\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
P=2r+r\theta .
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $144$ square units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
144={r}^{2}\frac{\theta }{2}.
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation and taking into account that $r>0,$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}144 & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta  \\ \theta  & =\frac{288}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2r+r\theta  \\  & =2r+r\cdot \frac{288}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =2r+\frac{288}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P,$ so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. Computing the derivative gives 

$$
{P}^{′}(r)=2-\frac{288}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{288}{{r}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2} & =288 \\ {r}^{2} & =144 \\ r & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=12$ is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative ${P}^{″}(r)=\frac{576}{{r}^{3}}>0$, the stationary point $r=12$ is a minimum.

Finally, when $r=12$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\frac{288}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{288}{144} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The dimensions of the circular sector with the smallest perimeter are $r=12$ and $\theta =2.$ Therefore, the smallest perimeter is 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2r+r\theta  \\  & =2\cdot 12+12\cdot 2 \\  & =24+24 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4d662c12-9d76-5b11-86a1-8fd56f6d8729" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4" :answer-field/id #uuid "8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4"] ["answer-bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43" :answer/id #uuid "bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43"] ["answer-bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43" :answer/value "48"] ["answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4" :answer-field/correct "answer-bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43"] ["answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4" :answer-field/choices "answer-bc531b63-ca0c-5196-ac8d-68aa088deb43"] ["question-4d662c12-9d76-5b11-86a1-8fd56f6d8729" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-8f1618c4-780a-57b4-9a0f-35ba97b75da4"] [17592186100837 :knowledge-point/questions "question-4d662c12-9d76-5b11-86a1-8fd56f6d8729"] ["question-92add898-4b49-5d01-bf37-847e609cbb26" :question/id #uuid "92add898-4b49-5d01-bf37-847e609cbb26"] ["question-92add898-4b49-5d01-bf37-847e609cbb26" :question/math-academy-id "q-15089"] ["question-92add898-4b49-5d01-bf37-847e609cbb26" :question/problem "![](images/c9/c9b79e710dda94e6c4d91a157317977f5b2388202bb63b08fcc325ea93f0453c.png)

$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\pi r+2x+2r \\  & =\pi r+2(\frac{25}{18r}-\frac{\pi r}{4})+2r \\  & =\pi r+\frac{25}{9r}-\frac{\pi r}{2}+2r \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)r+\frac{25}{9r}.\end{aligned}

Matt is planning a field whose surface is made up of a rectangle and two semicircles, as shown in the diagram. The area of the field must be $9\,{km}^{2}.$ What should be the radius $r$ if Matt wants a field with the smallest possible perimeter? Do not round the answer.

$\text{km}$"] ["question-b59b20a8-8e7c-533f-bc4e-e028196934bf" :question/worked-solution "We let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector (the same for both semicircles) and let $x$ be the other side of the rectangle. Then, we want to minimize the perimeter

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2x+\pi r+\pi r \\  & =2x+2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $9$ square units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
9=2rx+\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

Now, by making $2x$ the subject of the constraint equation and taking into account that $r>0,$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =2rx+\pi {r}^{2} \\ 2rx & =9-\pi {r}^{2} \\ 2x & =\frac{9}{r}-\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{9}{r}-\pi r+2\pi r \\  & =\frac{9}{r}+\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P,$ so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. Computing the derivative gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(r) & =-\frac{9}{{r}^{2}}+\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{9}{{r}^{2}}+\pi  & =0 \\ \pi  & =\frac{9}{{r}^{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{9}{\pi } \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{\pi }} \\ r & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $\frac{3}{\sqrt{\pi }}$ is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative ${P}^{″}(r)=\frac{18}{{r}^{3}}>0,$ the stationary point $r=\frac{3}{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{km}$ is a minimum."] ["question-b59b20a8-8e7c-533f-bc4e-e028196934bf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796" :answer-field/id #uuid "5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796"] ["answer-1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305" :answer/id #uuid "1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305"] ["answer-1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305" :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{\pi}}"] ["answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796" :answer-field/correct "answer-1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305"] ["answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796" :answer-field/choices "answer-1c220bd5-a7c3-540a-9148-f781412b5305"] ["question-b59b20a8-8e7c-533f-bc4e-e028196934bf" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-5de83ee2-eca3-5af9-9209-a72f1eca0796"] [17592186100837 :knowledge-point/questions "question-b59b20a8-8e7c-533f-bc4e-e028196934bf"] ["question-3990dbc6-49ea-5002-bf6b-028dcf68d1bf" :question/id #uuid "3990dbc6-49ea-5002-bf6b-028dcf68d1bf"] ["question-3990dbc6-49ea-5002-bf6b-028dcf68d1bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-345016"] ["question-3990dbc6-49ea-5002-bf6b-028dcf68d1bf" :question/problem "![](images/0e/0ef7a2645946099b10772fdc3fee46c582ad43debb0cb53041c46aa99c203ab1.png)

$$
P=2r+r\theta .
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $121$ square units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
121=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation and taking into account that $r>0,$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}121 & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta  \\ \theta  & =\frac{242}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2r+r\theta  \\  & =2r+r\cdot \frac{242}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =2r+\frac{242}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P,$ so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. Computing the derivative gives

$$
{P}^{′}(r)=2-\frac{242}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{242}{{r}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2} & =242 \\ {r}^{2} & =121 \\ r & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=11$ is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative ${P}^{″}(r)=\frac{484}{{r}^{3}}>0,$ the stationary point $r=11$ is a minimum.

Therefore, the radius of the circular sector with the smallest perimeter is $r=11$ units."] ["question-7c9b4d08-b984-5348-9fbd-0d702cd0c142" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0" :answer-field/id #uuid "d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0"] ["answer-7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685" :answer/id #uuid "7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685"] ["answer-7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685" :answer/value "11"] ["answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0" :answer-field/correct "answer-7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685"] ["answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0" :answer-field/choices "answer-7f9b529d-152c-55af-89ef-1953f5ea8685"] ["question-7c9b4d08-b984-5348-9fbd-0d702cd0c142" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-d7dafff5-b3a8-518e-8b51-5bc2eaf0b1e0"] [17592186100837 :knowledge-point/questions "question-7c9b4d08-b984-5348-9fbd-0d702cd0c142"] [17592186102009 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to solve problems involving sectors of circles, such as finding the maximum area of the sector of a circle given a fixed perimeter. "question-c57b9d4a-351a-58d6-893f-d761a9a6ee5e"] [17592186125830 :tutorial/content "A **cylinder** is a surface made by the set of lines that pass through a plane curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane and are perpendicular to this plane. The curve $C$ is called the **base curve**.

The familiar two-dimensional conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) can be used to describe cylinders. In this lesson, we'll explore these shapes.

An **elliptic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is an ellipse. If the ellipse lies in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of our elliptic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse $C.$ In particular, if $a=b$, we get a **circular cylinder.**

**Watch out!** This may look like the equation of a regular ellipse. However, since we're now describing a surface in three-dimensional space, we assume that the $z$-coordinate is arbitrary. Thus, if we want $z$ to feature in our equations explicitly, we would write

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k\in \mathbb R.$ 

For example, the graph of the elliptic cylinder

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. The center of its base ellipse $C$ is at the origin, and the **axis** of the elliptic cylinder (the line through the center of the cylinder) is the $z$-axis.

![](images/50/504e609e134654d258378226d90f5faa8b9f6d12313a4fcac4a23d0bfe6bea52.png)

Let's describe some properties of this elliptic cylinder:

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1,
$$

which is the base ellipse $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0)$ with semi-major and semi-minor axes of lengths $2$ and $1,$ respectively.

![](images/d0/d0e4c0630b0da60c4324330211ab1bf8090ebec067d9ebc2ac2a03056c500bd6.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/38/3813a5f43319056be03ddd8b3353ef3a8166b7495b32397c91066f40d0b33cd5.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $yz$-plane.

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(x+1)+1}{x+1})}^{2x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x+1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-00868e65-0caa-53d3-bac1-8c3f5e5b6143" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9e72dc91-9bb2-5a52-9ea8-c8a3392b078f" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x}.$"] ["question-981ba9c5-75b9-5f37-b62a-2b2258f28bdb" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x}={1}^{\infty },
$$

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-981ba9c5-75b9-5f37-b62a-2b2258f28bdb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ac530e0e-d3d1-5a9a-9415-9ac86edc2ff1" :answer-field/id #uuid }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1}.$"] ["question-c8a37d3e-d129-5ae7-8ba8-cbd709bbd8bf" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(2x-2)+1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $2(x-1)=n$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-1) & =n \\ x-1 & =\frac{n}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/2} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={e}^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c8a37d3e-d129-5ae7-8ba8-cbd709bbd8bf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c7bcd67e-475b-5366-91b7-b32feba0f989" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e

$$

{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{x} & =\frac{1}{n} \\ x & =3n.\end{aligned}

"answer-field-98fc00d4-eaa0-5074-a7a2-52d9b8beb28f"] [17592186059869 :knowledge-point/questions "question-38f4d55c-c716-54e2-ab1e-afc12e3f81f0"] [17592186060871 :tutorial/content "A situation involves **exponential decay** if some initial amount repeatedly shrinks due to being multiplied by some constant rate.

For example, suppose that a certain battery had a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V}$ when it was healthy. Following a sharp impact, the battery's voltage decreased by $\dfrac12$ every day since the day of the impact. What was the voltage of the battery $3$ days after it was damaged?

Starting with a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V},$ we know that this number will halve every day. So after $1$ day, the voltage (measured in volts) was

$$
{\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}.
$$

On the second day, this number halved again. So the voltage after $2$ days was

$$
\left({\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}\right)\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}.
$$

After one more day, the number above halves once again. So the voltage after $3$ days was

$$
{\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{black}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3}}.
$$

If we evaluate the above expression, we get:

$$
4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3 = 4\cdot \dfrac 1 8 =  \dfrac 1 2
$$

So after $3$ days, the voltage reduced to just $\dfrac 1 2\,\textrm{V}.$

This is an example of exponential decay. The voltage decreases by $\dfrac 1 2$ over a time interval of $1$ day, every day. The voltage decays very rapidly, as we can see from the graph below.

![](images/ee/ee97a0d5495dd28c8e0af1168fa4dc0455f1985ca8ab8f9a8e8dbf3e1a84ae99.png)"] [17592186059879 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186231575 :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$

$$

on $[-3,3]$, where $f$ is $6$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}"] [17592186231575 :question/worked-solution "Because $f$ is $6$-periodic on $[-3,3]$, we have $L=3$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$

$$"] ["question-a25da531-efbb-5c52-a54e-e70d588e0c03" :question/worked-solution "We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use $y(1)=6$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 6 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ B & =\frac{6}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$

(Figure not drawn to scale)"] ["question-e5a09c22-28d0-55d4-9b16-abdb75945ec5" :question/worked-solution "The area of the triangle is defined as 

$$
A=\frac{b\cdot h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the base is $b=AB,$ and the corresponding height is 

$$
h=CH=14\,m.
$$

Therefore, using the formula for the area, we can solve for the base as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 140 & =\frac{b\cdot 14}{2} \\ 280 & =b\cdot 14 \\ b & =\frac{280}{14} \\ b & =20\,m\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $AB=20\,m$ and hence, we have

$$
HB=AB-AH=20-15=5\,m.
$$"] ["question-e5a09c22-28d0-55d4-9b16-abdb75945ec5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e6c4c9c5-20e2-5ad2-b45c-aab945f75318" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1,
$$

and an elliptic cylinder, whose axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ in the $xy$-plane, is given by

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Thus, our equation is an elliptic cylinder with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(1,2),\,a=\frac{1}{5},\,b=\frac{1}{4}.
$$"] ["question-fcd8e2d4-6c09-5241-9d34-1a3c5fb626c5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ca554985-239e-5793-9c9c-69a9311b055f" :answer-field/id #uuid Also, recall the following from previous lessons:

- We can generate paraboloids, hyperboloids, and cones with alternative orientation axes by permuting the variables in the corresponding equation. 

For example, the equation of an elliptic cone with its vertex at $O$ and axis of symmetry along the $y$-axis is given by

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.
$$

- We can shift the center/vertex/saddle point of a quadric surface to $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ using the usual coordinate transformation:

$$
(x,y,z) \longrightarrow (x-x_0,y-y_0,z-z_0)
$$

Finally, there is a simple way to distinguish between hyperboloids with one and two sheets by simply looking at the equations:

- *one* minus sign indicates hyperboloids of *one* sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1
$$

- *two* minus signs indicate hyperboloids of *two* sheets:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-}1
$$"] [17592186125883 :tutorial/content "A table showing the most common cylinders whose base curve is centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane is given below.

"question-74d5d63f-ce92-5d6a-9703-105dc97e875a"] [17592186055982 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the following system of equations:
![](images/01/01eee66dd39797b90503716f097ff604a4f339d8ea0a25ceef9b8ea7a0898ab4.svg)

To solve systems of equations *graphically*, we first draw each of the equations in the same coordinate system. Then, the solution of the system is given by the common points where the lines intersect.

Let's see how this method works for the system above. To plot the functions given by the equations, we first rewrite them by making ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg) the subject in each equation.
![](images/c7/c7778dd2c82032ef68ad8221a990abe1b2bafb4e36a7a0e2640a43856be58c5a.svg) 

Then, we draw the lines in the same coordinate system:

![](images/47/47fb02cf8bb4668b24034302fd4265ec5261f4d244cd9d9d599afeffd91d2424.png)

The lines intersect at the point ![](images/d8/d87c68d6226f4bb9ecf52ab576a5ac45c83fbb02c83edd1af04ac235dd518467.svg), which is the solution to our system.

![](images/b3/b3b95135ad9a758f891280b15e8bd6f6165bf9f47a76a1c99280af02dad78911.png)

We can also use the graphical method to solve systems of equations where the corresponding functions are not straight lines. These types of systems are called **nonlinear systems**. Let's consider such an example."] [17592186054864 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836" :question/id #uuid "5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836"] ["question-5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836" :question/math-academy-id "q-337475"] ["question-5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3-3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3-3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3-3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5fdf7d2e-21a5-5a00-afb9-716691a79836" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a17ac1c5-d149-5ebf-8927-158723ddb605" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-adce0112-6117-576f-afb6-900e0d57f067" :question/math-academy-id "q-337526"] ["question-adce0112-6117-576f-afb6-900e0d57f067" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-adce0112-6117-576f-afb6-900e0d57f067" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x=\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\  & =16{e}^{-4x}(\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}) \\  & =8{e}^{-4x}({e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}) \\  & =8-8{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =8-8{e}^{-8x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 8-8{e}^{-8x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =8x+{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =8x{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-adce0112-6117-576f-afb6-900e0d57f067" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d9324986-dc8e-56cf-affb-81d9274ea958" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y={x}^{2}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-5753a7d8-bd1a-52e7-a471-c1acec6a4f75" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{2x})}^{′}-2(u{e}^{2x}) & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x}-2u{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}({x}^{2}) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{2x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5753a7d8-bd1a-52e7-a471-c1acec6a4f75" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fbadbf3f-b18a-5a99-9826-e9ff4c997442" :answer-field/id #uuid $$"] [17592186147207 :question/problem "The number of members $m$ of a club after $t$ years is given by the formula

$$

If there were $766$ members initially, and the number of members decreases by $22\%$ each year, what is the missing value in the expression for $m(t)?$"] [17592186147207 :question/worked-solution "The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay rate $r$) is

$$
m(t) = a(1-r)^t.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=766$ is the initial number of members.

- $r = 0.22$ is the decay rate ($22\%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in years.

$$

$$

In the beginning, there were $3\,000$ bacteria. After introducing the substance, Ralf noticed that the number of bacteria reduces by $\frac{1}{4}$ every minute.

The function $y(t)$ models the number of bacteria after $t$ minutes and is given by

$$
y(t)=3\,000\cdot {(\text{___})}^{t}.
$$

What number is missing?"] ["question-87d542d6-aac4-513b-9fc9-107312f9fcdf" :question/worked-solution "If the number of alive bacteria reduces by $\frac{1}{4}$ every minute, then $\frac{3}{4}$ of the bacteria remains every minute. So the decay factor is $\frac{3}{4}.$

The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay factor $b$) is

$$
y=a{b}^{t}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=3\,000$ is the initial number of bacteria.

- $b=\frac{3}{4}$ is the decay factor.

- $t=$ the time, in minutes.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=3\,000\cdot {(\frac{3}{4})}^{t}.
$$

So the missing number is $\frac{3}{4}.$"] ["question-87d542d6-aac4-513b-9fc9-107312f9fcdf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-97c59463-67ac-5c37-b808-28ec533a2185" $$

If the investment value is reduced by $\frac{1}{8},$ then $\frac{7}{8}$ of its value remained every month. So the decay factor is $\frac{7}{8}.$

The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay factor $b$) is

$$
p=a{b}^{t}.
$$

- $a=11\,280$ is the initial investment.

- $b=\frac{7}{8}$ is the decay factor.

- $t=$ the time, in months.

Therefore, the correct expression for $p(t)$ is

$$
p(t)=11\,280\cdot {(\frac{7}{8})}^{t}.
$$

So the missing number is $\frac{7}{8}.$"] ["question-ec5e8c7c-c10d-59da-bddc-7ee7a7739de6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-f4450d37-cda0-50d9-ad71-0e2c1df13152" exponential decay situation, it is often useful to start by setting up a function which represents the exponential decay. Then, we can evaluate that function as needed.

For example, suppose that a car's value depreciates by one-fifth every year. If the car was purchased for $\[math]25\,000,$ then what function gives the car's value after $t$ years? 

First, note that if the car's value reduces by $\dfrac 1 5$ every year, then $\dfrac 4 5$ of its value remains every year.

Let's write down what we know:

- $a = 25\,000$ is the **initial value** of the car (in dollars).

- $b = \dfrac 4 5$ is the **decay factor**.

- $t=$ the time, in years.

Let $y(t)$ be the car's value after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = ab^t.
$$

Substituting our values for $a$ and $b,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 25\,000\left(\dfrac 4 5\right)^t.
$$

To find the value of the car after $5$ years, we substitute $t=5$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(5)=25\,000\cdot {(\frac{4}{5})}^{5}=8\,192\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the car will be worth $\[/math] 8\,192$ in $5$ years."] [17592186148688 :tutorial/content "It's common to use a **decay rate** (rather than a decay factor) when describing exponential decay. A decay rate is typically expressed using a percent.

For example, suppose that after treatment with a particular antibiotic, the number of infected cells in a specimen decreased by $30\%$ per hour. If there were approximately $5$ million infected cells at the beginning of the treatment, how many infected cells remained after $3$ hours?

Let $y(t)$ be the number of infected cells after $t$ hours. The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay rate $r$) is

$$
y = a(1-r)^t.
$$

Notice that this is very similar to the formula for exponential growth. The difference here is that we have a minus $(-)$ instead of a plus $(+)$ in the parentheses.

In our case, we have:

- $a=5$ is the initial number of infected cells (in millions).

- $r = 0.30$ is the decay rate ($30\%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in hours.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y(t)$ is

$$
y  = 5(1-0.3)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above gives

$$
y(t) =5(0.7)^{t}.
$$

Evaluating the function for $t=3$ hours, we get

$$
y(3) = 5(0.7)^{3} = 1.715.
$$

Therefore, after $3$ hours, there were $1.715$ million infected cells.

When writing down a formula for exponential decay, the key takeaway is this:

- If we're given a **decay rate** (usually expressed as a percent), then we use the formula $y(t) = a(1-r)^t.$

- If we're given a **decay factor**, then we use the formula $y(t) = ab^t.$"] [17592186147672 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186114950 :question/problem "A house was purchased for $\[math]90\,000.$ Shortly after purchasing the property, the owners discovered widening cracks in the foundation. :question/problem "The caffeine level, in milligrams, in a patient's bloodstream $t$ hours after drinking a cup of coffee is given by the function $C(t)=140\cdot {(0.9)}^{t}.$ How much caffeine is metabolized between the second and third hour after drinking the coffee?"] ["question-bce8526b-2382-5fd4-882b-274b4364bd61" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the level of caffeine in the blood between $t=2$ and $t=3$ hours after drinking a cup of coffee. To calculate this, we find the level of caffeine in the blood after $2$ hours, and we subtract from it the level of caffeine in the blood after $3$ hours. So we need to evaluate

$$
C(2)-C(3).
$$

The level of caffeine in the blood after $2$ hours is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C(2) & =140\cdot {(0.9)}^{2} \\  & =140\cdot 0.81 \\  & =113.4.\end{aligned}
$$

The level of caffeine in the blood after $3$ hours is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C(3) & =140\cdot {(0.9)}^{3} \\  & =140\cdot 0.729 \\  & =102.06.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the level of caffeine metabolized between $t=2$ and $t=3$ hours after drinking a cup of coffee is

$$
113.4-102.06=11.34.
$$"] ["question-bce8526b-2382-5fd4-882b-274b4364bd61" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-73fafd4e-edd5-5743-8519-b748f97293c4" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The daily number of customers to a particular cafe declines according to the expression $500\cdot (0.83)^{t}$, where $t$ is the number of days since the local news reported that the cafe did not pass a health inspection. 
What does the base of the exponential expression $(0.83)$ mean in this context?"] ["question-8a688991-2eb3-5f8d-836d-4a680ceee3ff" :question/worked-solution "The given expression is an exponential decay expression of the form $y(t)=a\cdot (1-r)^{t},$ where:

- $a=500$ represents the initial number of customers.

- $1-r=0.83,$ where $r$ is the decay rate.

- $t$ is the time in days since the local news reported that the cafe did not pass a health inspection.

Solving for $r,$ we get

$$
1-r=0.83\,⟹\,r=0.17.
$$

Now, $0.17$ (expressed as a percent) is equal to $17%.$ 

So, the base of the exponential expression $0.83$ means that the number of customers decreases by $17%$ every day."] ["question-8a688991-2eb3-5f8d-836d-4a680ceee3ff" :question/difficulty - $a=20\,000$ represents the initial number of ticks.

- $1-r=0.7,$ where $r$ is the decay rate.

- $t$ is the time, in weeks, since the acaricides were first applied.

Solving for $r,$ we get

$$
1-r=0.7\,⟹\,r=0.3.
$$

Now, $0.3$ (expressed as a percent) is equal to $30%.$ 

So, the base of the exponential expression $0.7$ means that the population of ticks decreases by $30%$ every week."] ["question-836a9482-113e-597c-80f8-a8ed0a6b01c8" :question/difficulty For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

$$
y(t) = a \cdot b^t.
$$

So, we can deduce the following:

- $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

["question-95921cae-0a0b-5427-8528-229b03960d35" :question/worked-solution "The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{1}{3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =c \\ c(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =1 \\ 3c{x}^{2}+c{y}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)$ can't be zero or negative. Therefore, we get a family of surfaces given by

$$
3c{x}^{2}+c{y}^{2}=1,\,c\in (0,\infty ).
$$"] ["question-95921cae-0a0b-5427-8528-229b03960d35" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-113c6c84-a326-59a4-aca0-106d9621d960" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Suppose that we want to make a box with a square base and without a lid using metal sheets. We have only $4 \, \textrm{m} ^ 2$ of sheet metal to create the box. Given that the volume of the box has been maximized, find the value of $x.$

![](images/68/6821176223c59c981ac57cfa754044a145754b747baf7985f7eefd073dcd8758.png)"] [17592186100648 :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the values of $x$ and $y$ such that the volume

$$
V = x\cdot x\cdot y = x^2 y
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: The surface area is $4 \, \textrm{m} ^ 2$. So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\eqalign{
 S &= \textrm{(area of the base) } + 4 \, \textrm{(area of one side) } \[5pt]
4 &= x^2 + 4 x y.}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject in the constraint equation: 

$$
y = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{4}
$$

Then, we substitute $y = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{4}$ in the expression $V=x^2y,$ and we get

$$
\eqalign{
V(x) &= x^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{4}\right) \[5pt]
&= x - \dfrac{x^3}{4}.
}
$$

 

**Step 4**: We solve the equation $V'(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
V'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{3x^2}{4},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\eqalign{
V'(x) &= 0 \[5pt]
1 - \dfrac{3x^2}{4} &=0 \[5pt]
x^2 &= \dfrac{4}{3} \[5pt]
x &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.
}
$$

Note that in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the side length $x$ must be positive. 

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
V''(x) = -\dfrac{3}{2}x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad V''\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3} < 0.
$$

Since $V''\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)$ is negative, we conclude that $x=\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ is indeed a maximum of $V(x).$

Therefore, the box with the largest possible volume has side length $x= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,\mathrm{m}.$"] [17592186100649 :question/problem "Consider a box with a square base with side lengths $x$ and height $y,$ as shown below. The volume of the box is $1$ cubic unit. Given that the surface area of the box has been minimized, find the value of $x.$

![](images/5f/5f852cff121a53206cdcfeb8f4a0efec5a43fd2ed73ab569ec537cbe896b405c.png)"] [17592186100649 :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $x$ such that the surface area

$$
S = 2x^2 + 4xy
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume is exactly $1$ cubic unit. So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot x\cdot y \\ 1 & ={x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $S,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2{x}^{2}+4xy \\  & =2{x}^{2}+4x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation $S'(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
S'(x) = 4x - \dfrac{4}{x^2},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 4x-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 4x & =\frac{4}{{x}^{2}} \\ 4{x}^{3} & =4 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=1$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
S''(x) = 4 + \frac{8}{x^3} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad S''(1) = 4 + 8 = 12 > 0.
$$

Since $S''\left(1\right)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=1$ is indeed a minimum of $S(x).$

Therefore, the box with the smallest possible surface area has side length $x= 1$ unit."] [17592186100771 :question/problem "A box with no lid and a square base has a manufacturing cost that depends on two materials. The material for the base costs $\[math]4$ per square meter, and the material for the lateral faces costs $\[/math]2$ per square meter. The box must have a volume of $8\,\mathrm{m^3}.$

What is the value of $x$ for the box that has the smallest production cost? 

![](images/a6/a6f83d3c86e6d5c2e470f68e2e75f32c2fb7573a08cc188d2fd7080103351076.png)"] [17592186100771 :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $x$ such that the manufacturing cost

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4{x}^{2}+2\cdot 4xy \\  & =4{x}^{2}+8xy\end{aligned}
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume must be $8\,\mathrm{m^3}.$ So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot x\cdot y \\ 8 & ={x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =8 \\ y & =\frac{8}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $C,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4{x}^{2}+8xy \\ C & =4{x}^{2}+8x\cdot \frac{8}{{x}^{2}} \\ C & =4{x}^{2}+\frac{64}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation $C'(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
C'(x) = 8x - \frac{64}{x^2},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 8x-\frac{64}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 8{x}^{3} & =64 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=2$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
C''(x) = 8 + \dfrac{128}{x^3} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad C''\left(2\right) > 0.
$$

Since $C''\left( 2\right)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=2$ is indeed a minimum of $C(x).$"] [17592186100770 :question/problem "A piece of cardboard measures $12\,\mathrm{cm}\times 8\, \mathrm{cm}.$ A tray of height $y\,\textrm{cm}$ is formed by cutting a $y\times y \,\textrm{cm}^2$ square from each of the corners and folding up the sides, as shown in the diagram. Determine the height of the box that gives the maximum possible volume. Round your answer to two decimal places.

![](images/4a/4a3bab5daf0f7426d5b2ddf418439d7c6b8a6651a3de7b17dcfcdf2f6616f898.png)"] [17592186100770 :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the values of $x, y,$ and $z$ such that the volume

$$
V = xyz
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: Notice that the width $x$ and the depth $z$ of the tray are given by

$$
x=12 - 2y,\qquad z=8-2y.
$$

 

Since $x > 0$ and $z > 0,$ we must have that $12-2y > 0$ and $8-2y >0$, hence $y<       4.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0 <             y <             4.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =xyz \\  & =(12-2y)(y)(8-2y) \\  & =4{y}^{3}-40{y}^{2}+96y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation $V'(y) = 0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
V'(y) = 12y^2 - 80y + 96,

$$
288=xy(\frac{x}{3})=\frac{{x}^{2}y}{3}.
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{3} & =288 \\ {x}^{2}y & =864 \\ y & =\frac{864}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $S,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2xz+2xy+2yz \\  & =2x(\frac{x}{3})+2x(\frac{864}{{x}^{2}})+2(\frac{864}{{x}^{2}})(\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{2}+\frac{1728}{x}+\frac{576}{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{2}+\frac{2304}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${S}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{S}^{′}(x)=\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ \frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{4}{3}x & =\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3}{x}^{3} & =2304 \\ {x}^{3} & =1728 \\ x & =12.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Consider a box with width $x,$ height $y,$ and depth $z,$ as shown above. The depth of the box is half its width. Given that the box's volume is $243$ cubic units, what is the smallest possible surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ of the box? Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}} square units"] ["question-e2adf7b9-c049-5411-a710-9c822b654299" :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $x$ such that the surface area

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume is $243$ cubic units. So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot y\cdot z \\ 243 & =xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that $z=\frac{x}{2},$ we get the constraint equation

$$
243=xy(\frac{x}{2})=\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}.
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2} & =243 \\ {x}^{2}y & =486 \\ y & =\frac{486}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $S,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2xz+2xy+2yz \\  & =2x(\frac{x}{2})+2x(\frac{486}{{x}^{2}})+2(\frac{486}{{x}^{2}})(\frac{x}{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+\frac{972}{x}+\frac{486}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}+\frac{1458}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${S}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{S}^{′}(x)=2x-\frac{1458}{{x}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-\frac{1458}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2x & =\frac{1458}{{x}^{2}} \\ 2{x}^{3} & =1458 \\ {x}^{3} & =729 \\ x & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=9$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{S}^{″}(x)=2+\frac{2916}{{x}^{3}}\,⟹\,{S}^{″}(9)=2+4=6>0.
$$

Since ${S}^{″}(9)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=9$ is indeed a minimum.

Now, the smallest surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ that the box can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\text{min}}=S(9) & ={9}^{2}+\frac{1458}{9} \\  & =243\,\text{square units}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e2adf7b9-c049-5411-a710-9c822b654299" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9" :answer-field/id #uuid "eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9"] ["answer-f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea" :answer/id #uuid "f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea"] ["answer-f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea" :answer/value "243"] ["answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9" :answer-field/correct "answer-f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea"] ["answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9" :answer-field/choices "answer-f7c8741a-939b-59a0-976b-bf72431b48ea"] ["question-e2adf7b9-c049-5411-a710-9c822b654299" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-eae4d3f6-b44e-59db-a081-02bc4a4fa2c9"] [17592186100839 :knowledge-point/questions "question-e2adf7b9-c049-5411-a710-9c822b654299"] ["question-5f708375-cdc1-53f8-8bb4-b17c1643502c" :question/id #uuid "5f708375-cdc1-53f8-8bb4-b17c1643502c"] ["question-5f708375-cdc1-53f8-8bb4-b17c1643502c" :question/math-academy-id "q-315628"] ["question-5f708375-cdc1-53f8-8bb4-b17c1643502c" :question/problem "![](images/85/8548c87f15edc7e7c903c753767f12bd6f4c6f0294ff07734659583907f2ea4a.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}2{z}^{2}y & =180 \\ y & =\frac{90}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $C,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =10xz+4xy+4yz \\  & =10(2z)z+4(2z)(\frac{90}{{z}^{2}})+4\,(\frac{90}{{z}^{2}})\,z \\  & =20{z}^{2}+\frac{720}{z}+\frac{360}{z} \\  & =20{z}^{2}+\frac{1080}{z}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${C}^{′}(z)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{C}^{′}(z)=40z-\frac{1080}{{z}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ 40z-\frac{1080}{{z}^{2}} & =0 \\ 40{z}^{3} & =1080 \\ {z}^{3} & =27 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{{field-1}} units"] ["question-caab3419-40f4-5f42-9fc6-7d0c53c70e6a" :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $x$ such that the manufacturing cost

$$

$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume must be $10\,{m}^{3}.$ So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot x\cdot y \\ 10 & ={x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =10 \\ y & =\frac{10}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $C,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =5{x}^{2}+8xy \\  & =5{x}^{2}+8x\cdot \frac{10}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =5{x}^{2}+\frac{80}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${C}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{C}^{′}(x)=10x-\frac{80}{{x}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 10x-\frac{80}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 10{x}^{3} & =80 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=2$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{C}^{″}(x)=10+\frac{160}{{x}^{3}}\,⟹\,{C}^{″}(2)=10+20=30>0.
$$

Since ${C}^{″}(2)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=2$ is indeed a minimum of $C(x).$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ 8z-\frac{216}{{z}^{2}} & =0 \\ 8{z}^{3} & =216 \\ {z}^{3} & =27 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $z=3$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{C}^{″}(z)=8+\frac{432}{{z}^{3}}\,⟹\,{C}^{″}(3)=8+16=24>0.
$$

Since ${C}^{″}(3)$ is positive, we conclude that $z=3$ is indeed a minimum of $C(z).$

$$
V=xyz
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: Notice that the width $x$ and the depth $z$ of the tray are given by

$$
x=15-2y,\,z=8-2y.
$$

 

Since $x>0$ and $z>0,$ we must have that $15-2y>0$ and $8-2y>0$, hence $y<4.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0<y<4.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =xyz \\  & =(15-2y)(y)(8-2y) \\  & =4{y}^{3}-46{y}^{2}+120y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=12{y}^{2}-92y+120,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 12{y}^{2}-92y+120 & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-23y+30 & =0 \\ (3y-5)(y-6) & =0 \\ y & =\frac{5}{3},\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $6$ since we already know that $0<y<4.$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $\frac{5}{3}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=24y-92.
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(\frac{5}{3})$ is negative, we conclude that $\frac{5}{3}$ is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

A piece of cardboard measures $10\,in\times 10\,in.$ A tray of height $y\,\text{in}$ is formed by cutting a $y\times y\,{\text{in}}^{2}$ square from each of the corners and folding up the sides, as shown in the diagram. Determine the height of the box that gives the maximum possible volume."] ["question-fcc5cb30-3a54-5c1c-aecb-10ee16fa7222" :question/worked-solution "**Step 1**: We need to find the values of $x$ and $y$ such that the volume

$$
V={x}^{2}y
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: Notice that the side length $x$ of the tray is given by

$$
x=10-2y.
$$

 

Since $x>0,$ we must have that $10-2y>0$ hence $y<5.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0<y<5.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{2}y \\  & =(10-2y)^{2}y \\  & =4{y}^{3}-40{y}^{2}+100y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=12{y}^{2}-80y+100,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 12{y}^{2}-80y+100 & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-20y+25 & =0 \\ (3y-5)(y-5) & =0 \\ y & =\frac{5}{3},\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $5$ since we already know that $0<y<5.$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $\frac{5}{3}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=24y-80.
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(\frac{5}{3})=-40$ is negative, we conclude that $\frac{5}{3}$ is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

Therefore, the stationary point $y=\frac{5}{3}$ gives the maximum possible volume."] ["question-fcc5cb30-3a54-5c1c-aecb-10ee16fa7222" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
V={x}^{2}y

is the greatest possible value.

$$

Since $x>0,$ we must have that $6-2y>0$ hence $y<3.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0<y<3.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{2}y \\  & =(6-2y)^{2}y \\  & =4{y}^{3}-24{y}^{2}+36y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=12{y}^{2}-48y+36,

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 12{y}^{2}-48y+36 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-4y+3 & =0 \\ (y-3)(y-1) & =0 \\ y & =3,\,1.\end{aligned}

We discard $3$ since we already know that $0<y<3.$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $1$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=24y-48.
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(1)=-24$ is negative, we conclude that $1$ is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

ourselves of the general strategy for optimization problems:

1\. Draw a diagram of the situation, introducing variables where necessary.

2\. Write down the equation of the quantity that you're trying to maximize or minimize. This is called the **objective function**, and it might include more than one variable.

3\. Write down the constraint equation.

4\. Use the constraint equation to write the objective function in terms of a single variable only.

5\. Differentiate the objective function, set it equal to zero, and solve for the stationary points.

6\. Test each stationary point using the second derivative test. Or you can use the first derivative test if it's easier.

We can use differentiation to solve optimization problems involving boxes and trays, such as maximizing a box's volume given a fixed amount of material."] [17592186101068 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0] ["question-87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e" :question/id #uuid "87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e"] ["question-87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-83831"] ["question-87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e" :question/problem "For the polynomial $f(x)=4{x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+x+1,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?"] ["question-87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $1,$ and its factors are $\pm 1.$

- The leading coefficient is $4,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2$ and $\pm 4.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This makes a total of $6$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 3=6.$)"] ["question-87021664-1460-517e-b0da-ae45fc0bbb9e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] *Hint: Eliminate the variable $q.$*"] ["question-4c472f9d-cfda-5414-a840-ee6d18544bcc" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the $q$-coefficient in the first equation is $2,$ while in the second equation it is $4.$ 

If we multiply the first equation by $-2,$ then the $q$-coefficient will become $-4,$ which will cancel with the coefficient of $4$ in the second equation.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(\,3p+2q=11\,)\,\times (-2) \\ 5p+4q=19\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-6p-4q=-22 \\ 5p+4q=19\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $q$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-6p-\cancel{4q} & =-22 \\ 5p+\cancel{4q} & =19 \\ (-6p+5p) & =(-22+19) \\ -p & =-3 \\ p & =3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $p=3.$ However, we still need to find $q.$ To do this, we substitute $p=3$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3p+2q & =11 \\ 3(3)+2q & =11 \\ 9+2q & =11 \\ 2q & =2 \\ q & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=3,\,q=1,$ which can be expressed as $(3,1).$"] ["question-4c472f9d-cfda-5414-a840-ee6d18544bcc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] For example, suppose that a certain battery had a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V}$ when it was healthy. Following a sharp impact, the battery's voltage decreased by

$$

every day since the day of the impact. What was the voltage of the battery $3$ days after it was damaged?

Starting with a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V}$, we know that this number will halve every day. So after $1$ day, the voltage (measured in volts) was

$$
{\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}
$$

On the second day, this number halved again. So the voltage after $2$ days was

$$
\left({\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}\right)\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}
$$

After one more day, the number above halves once again. So the voltage after $3$ days was

$$
{\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{black}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3}}
$$

If we evaluate the above expression, we get:

$$
4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3 = 4\cdot \dfrac 1 8 = \dfrac 1 2
$$

So after $3$ days, the voltage reduced to just

$$
\dfrac 1 2\,\textrm{V}
$$

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

For example, suppose that a car's value depreciates by one-fifth every year. If the car was purchased for $\[math]25\,000$, then what function gives the car's value after $t$ years?

- $t=$ the time, in years.

Let $y(t)$ be the car's value after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = ab^t
$$

$$

$$

To find the value of the car after $5$ years, we substitute $t=5$ into the above:

Therefore, the car will be worth $\[/math] 8\,192$ in $5$ years."] [17592186148688 :tutorial/content "It's common to use a **decay rate** (rather than a decay factor) when describing exponential decay. A decay rate is typically expressed using a percent.

For example, suppose that after treatment with a particular antibiotic, the number of infected cells in a specimen decreased by $30\%$ per hour. If there were approximately $5$ million infected cells at the beginning of the treatment, how many infected cells remained after $3$ hours?

Let $y(t)$ be the number of infected cells after $t$ hours. The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay rate $r$) is

$$
y = a(1-r)^t
$$

Notice that this is very similar to the formula for exponential growth. The difference here is that we have a minus $(-)$ instead of a plus $(+)$ in the parentheses.

In our case, we have:

- $a=5$ is the initial number of infected cells (in millions).
- $r = 0.30$ is the decay rate ($30\%$ expressed as a decimal).
- $t=$ the time, in hours.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y(t)$ is

$$
y = 5(1-0.3)^{t}
$$

Simplifying the above gives

$$
y(t) =5(0.7)^{t}
$$

Evaluating the function for $t=3$ hours, we get

$$
y(3) = 5(0.7)^{3} = 1.715
$$

Therefore, after $3$ hours, there were $1.715$ million infected cells.

When writing down a formula for exponential decay, the key takeaway is this:

- If we're given a **decay rate** (usually expressed as a percent), then we use the formula $y(t) = a(1-r)^t$.
- If we're given a **decay factor**, then we use the formula $y(t) = ab^t$."] [17592186114950 :question/problem "A house was purchased for $\[math]90\,000$. {(x + 2y = 1; (x - y =-2)\cdot (-1)

3y &= 3 \\
y &= 1
\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360563 :question/id #uuid "b3f6701f-c993-5ff2-926d-7219617af2de" :question/math-academy-id "q-95109"} {:db/id 17592186360564 :question/id #uuid the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =0\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360567 :question/id #uuid "09b6c584-862f-5f2c-8d59-a960b719bfdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-95116" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124594 :knowledge-point/id #uuid for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360581 :question/id #uuid "2f89a4f6-9145-5fdf-84a8-9fcaed162c54" :question/math-academy-id "q-95171"} {:db/id 17592186360582 :question/id #uuid 17592186125534 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125838 :tutorial/content "Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. 

The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "733b56f3-7c9a-59a6-bc6b-ef87bf07d149" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4975 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Cylindrical Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "f4acd445-680f-5872-a4a3-6bda4e7738eb" :step/math-academy-id 30978 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125535}} {:db/id 17592186125535 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124596 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124407 :question/id #uuid "c1e69bbe-b079-56e5-9ce0-296785d73100" :question/math-academy-id "e-8296"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2ee45610-e14c-593e-9002-e2b2fcdb4517" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125243} {:db/id 17592186125248} {:db/id 17592186360581} {:db/id 17592186360582} {:db/id 17592186360583} {:db/id 17592186367921} {:db/id 17592186368892} {:db/id 17592186479084} {:db/id 17592186479097} {:db/id 17592186479112} {:db/id 17592186479138} {:db/id 17592186479141}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Cylindrical Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "19fc48bd-f02a-5fc4-8b9f-23e3d17412b2" :step/math-academy-id 30979 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125563}} {:db/id 17592186125562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125847 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$

For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e3237863-f115-5396-a03f-fd481d101761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5358 :tutorial/title "Differentiating of a Function Given in Polar Coordinates With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "443067c1-4f4c-574c-818f-cec45ee26f17" :step/math-academy-id 33488 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125533}} {:db/id 17592186125563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125848 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e3237863-f115-5396-a03f-fd481d101761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5358 :tutorial/title "Differentiating of a Function Given in Polar Coordinates With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186125848 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$
