:knowledge-point/id #uuid "85c79564-93e7-5054-9534-71dc8dc54f7b" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Rectangle or a Square Given Its Perimeter"}] :question/problem "Find the area of the rectangle $ABCD$ if its perimeter is $40$ and ${BC} = 12$." :question/worked-solution "We can find the length of ${AB}$ by using the formula for the perimeter, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p &= AB + BC + CD + DA \\
p &= 2AB + 2BC \\
40 &= 2AB + 2(12) \\
40 &= 2AB + 24 \\
2AB &= 16 \\
AB &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the rectangle $ABCD$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= AB \cdot BC \\
&= 8 \cdot 12 \\
&= 96
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048360} {:db/id 17592186048921} {:db/id 17592186106186 :question/id #uuid "a21b0be4-2473-5f6a-9528-3bf7bcd2c891" :question/math-academy-id "q-21439"} {:db/id 17592186106187 :question/id #uuid "4d7bbcd5-42fc-570d-9c09-f86ca447d81d" :question/math-academy-id "q-21449"} {:db/id 17592186105930 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105534 :question/id #uuid "f7dc8ebd-817d-5709-99a5-f21dc726c2d0" :question/math-academy-id "e-2936"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "305f1d10-f98a-5849-a566-549265b3508d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050428} {:db/id 17592186050792}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106409 :question/id #uuid "cdc19067-6cda-515c-a2cb-3e0a9adb135c" :question/math-academy-id "q-53234"} {:db/id 17592186106418 :question/id #uuid "dd8925d2-a6fd-5eb6-9b33-c6c560728cdc" :question/math-academy-id "q-53274"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Square From a Diagram"} {:db/id 17592186105534 :question/id #uuid "f7dc8ebd-817d-5709-99a5-f21dc726c2d0" :question/math-academy-id "e-2936" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186105930 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "305f1d10-f98a-5849-a566-549265b3508d" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Square From a Diagram"}] :question/problem "What is the area of the square shown below?

![](images/53/53ab7a043ebbe03245fd0f8e1bf6438897a30d91654b6e51194205e4c302c07f.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area of a square with sides of length $a$ is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a^2
$$

Note that each side of a grid cell measures $3\,\textrm{ft}$, and each side of the shaded square covers $4$ grid cells. So, the length of each side of the shaded square is

$$
a = 3 \times 4 = 12 \, \textrm{ft}
$$

Therefore, the area of the shaded square is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= a^{2} = 12^{2} = 144ft^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050428} {:db/id 17592186050792} {:db/id 17592186106409 :question/id #uuid "cdc19067-6cda-515c-a2cb-3e0a9adb135c" :question/math-academy-id "q-53234"} {:db/id 17592186106418 :question/id #uuid "dd8925d2-a6fd-5eb6-9b33-c6c560728cdc" :question/math-academy-id "q-53274"} {:db/id 17592186105932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105537 :question/id #uuid "cf89adb1-3344-5ed4-b2e0-48506af917bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-2940"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8e574a9-a37d-512f-aa4d-543ad1a3de84" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106408 :question/id #uuid "c5a4869d-3fd9-58cb-87a6-106a1d7534aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-53232"} {:db/id 17592186106415 :question/id #uuid "b12f2808-eb9d-5f00-b03a-649e31599d42" :question/math-academy-id "q-53262"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Rectangle From a Diagram"} {:db/id 17592186105537 :question/id #uuid "cf89adb1-3344-5ed4-b2e0-48506af917bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-2940" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186105932 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8e574a9-a37d-512f-aa4d-543ad1a3de84" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Rectangle From a Diagram"}] :question/problem "A cinema has a rectangular hall whose dimensions are shown in the figure below. What is the area of the hall?

![](images/e7/e7263eb3d75ecb243301c2d6c5712dd77232b97b6839123febec3260b389b2e6.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area of a rectangle is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a \cdot b
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the lengths of the sides.

From the figure, we obtain that

$$
a = 4.5\,\mathrm{m}, \qquad b = 6\,\mathrm{m}
$$

Therefore, the area of the hall is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= a \cdot b = 4.5 \cdot 6 = 27m^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106408 :question/id #uuid "c5a4869d-3fd9-58cb-87a6-106a1d7534aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-53232"} {:db/id 17592186106415 :question/id #uuid "b12f2808-eb9d-5f00-b03a-649e31599d42" :question/math-academy-id "q-53262"} {:db/id 17592186105935 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105538 :question/id #uuid "022da369-7dfd-5865-8e72-4317203ad11e" :question/math-academy-id "e-2941"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0726a51-b1a9-5755-a19b-0cc68f96b875" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106416 :question/id #uuid "b96e524d-8067-5f5c-9997-cc35f0bb446f" :question/math-academy-id "q-53269"} {:db/id 17592186106417 :question/id #uuid "8ccd7928-e787-5f54-b334-1417aba9f46a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53272"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of a Side of a Rectangle Given Another Side and Its Area"} {:db/id 17592186105538 :question/id #uuid "022da369-7dfd-5865-8e72-4317203ad11e" :question/math-academy-id "e-2941" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186105935 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0726a51-b1a9-5755-a19b-0cc68f96b875" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of a Side of a Rectangle Given Another Side and Its Area"}] :question/problem "The area of the rectangular field shown below is $2\,400\,\textrm{m}^2$. What is the value of $x$?

![](images/94/9419ae4a3099216109bff99906e5d1724a8f01f61e48e22edc62c0e1b62a1bef.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area of a rectangle is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a \cdot b
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the lengths of the sides.

From the figure, we obtain that

$$
\mathcal{A} = 2\,400\mathrm{m}^2, \qquad a = 60\,\mathrm{m}, \qquad b=x
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= a \cdot b \\
2400 &= 60 \cdot x \\
x &= \frac{2400}{60} \\
x &= 40m
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106416 :question/id #uuid "b96e524d-8067-5f5c-9997-cc35f0bb446f" :question/math-academy-id "q-53269" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105935 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0726a51-b1a9-5755-a19b-0cc68f96b875" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of a Side of a Rectangle Given Another Side and Its Area"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93e527b0-2bf3-54a5-b426-ce2db70bfcda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "30yd" :db/id 17592186104645} {:answer/id #uuid "b5824ac9-b253-5d61-a72f-03f4ab1b6cb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "15yd^{2}" :db/id 17592186104646} {:answer/id #uuid "bd6c2a3a-91d5-5a6d-b6ab-137512bea2b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "500yd" :db/id 17592186104647} {:answer/id #uuid "e42c544a-d7ee-5e22-9fc0-9397724c210f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "20yd" :db/id 17592186104648} {:answer/id #uuid "7221319a-1f89-594b-ad8f-1b012fe3d95f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "25yd" :db/id 17592186104649}] :answer-field/id #uuid "2dfd1944-ce2e-5b28-a2cd-855b60691175" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186104644}] :question/problem "![](images/91/91a554b467201b7507b531dcc0b6e1d5d9970d3e6d6554878644a31e5e38d9fa.png)

[{:db/id 17592186106796 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105838 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105671 :question/id #uuid "08cf33de-c71e-55bb-8906-112075c06a37" :question/math-academy-id "e-7691"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "85c79564-93e7-5054-9534-71dc8dc54f7b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048360} {:db/id 17592186048921}] "470f5ea9-9e6d-525a-95cd-a5d8c2257844" :step/math-academy-id 28598} {:db/id 17592186106964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107049 :tutorial/content "The **area** of a shape is a measure of how much space is enclosed by a shape on a plane. Let's consider a square with sides of length of $1\,\textrm{in}$.

![](images/bc/bc59b6e5a60a2f22e6c7fb102eba2f255dd09e115fd04a16050570f9f8b053f4.png)

The area of this square is equal to ${\color{red}{1\,\textrm{in}^2}}$, which we say in words as "one square inch."

Similarly, if we have three squares with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$, $1\,\textrm{m}$, and $1\,\textrm{ft}$ respectively, then their respective areas will be
$1\,\textrm{cm}^2, \qquad 1\,\textrm{m}^2, \qquad 1\,\textrm{ft}^2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1b7b7096-09d8-55d7-a7bc-45c3a83c9412" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2302 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b19100e-d452-53e4-9fd7-da598e7cbf2e" :step/math-academy-id 9594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106965}} {:db/id 17592186106965 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107050 :tutorial/content "Let's now suppose that we would like to compute the area of the square $ABCD$, shown below. Notice that, this time, the sides of the square span multiple unit lengths.

![](images/14/1441893036f9a41ed0daa8c8ce078d6a733bab5bb88dc60259a6b9ebc1c2e7c0.png)

The length of one side of a grid square is equal to $1\,\textrm{cm}$. So, the area of one grid square is $1\,\textrm{cm}^2$.

Now, we need to find how many grid squares are contained inside $ABCD$.

![](images/5f/5f293762b05013689996298a7804fb5f507eb228112397641fb8f662ff74ba49.png)

Inside the large blue square, there are $3$ rows containing $3$ grid squares each, so we can fit exactly

$$
3 \times 3 = 3^2 = 9
$$

grid squares inside $ABCD$.

Each grid square has area $1\,\textrm{cm}^2$, so the area $\mathcal A$ of $ABCD$ is

$$
\mathcal{A} = (3\,\textrm{cm})^2 = 9\,\textrm{cm}^2
$$

In general, if we have a square with a side of length $a$, then the area of the square is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a^2
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5e28b50-44b1-59d2-a7d6-e3ffb7a10038" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2303 :tutorial/title "The Area of a Square"} :step/id #uuid "e7fe8167-acaa-551f-8d92-567afcc40716" :step/math-academy-id 9595 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106967}} {:db/id 17592186106967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105930 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105534 :question/id #uuid "f7dc8ebd-817d-5709-99a5-f21dc726c2d0" :question/math-academy-id "e-2936"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "305f1d10-f98a-5849-a566-549265b3508d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050428} {:db/id 17592186050792}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106409} {:db/id 17592186106418}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Square From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "fc7ddcc6-0df2-5e0c-8bc0-d2a0e1080407" :step/math-academy-id 9597 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106969}} {:db/id 17592186106969 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107052 :tutorial/content "In general, for a rectangle with sides of length $a$ and $b$, the area of the rectangle is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a \cdot b
$$

Let's demonstrate by finding the area of the rectangle $PQRS$, shown below.

![](images/a0/a0890441b4c7e888ca7ede71a075825ca6700f79d242d1dec7e35ab2d787e5e0.png)

From the figure, we see that the rectangle has the following side lengths:

$$
a = {PQ} = 10\,\mathrm{cm}, \qquad b = {PS} = 6\,\mathrm{cm}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= a \cdot b \\
&= 10cm \cdot 6cm \\
&= 60cm^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

It does not matter which side we call $a$ and which side we call $b$. In the above example, if we set

$$
a = {QR} = 6\,\mathrm{cm}, \qquad b = {RS} = 10\,\mathrm{cm}
$$

then we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= a \cdot b \\
&= 10cm \cdot 6cm \\
&= 60cm^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

as before." :tutorial/id #uuid "2dff044c-7f7f-5531-8db6-05e1e8b7be7c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2305 :tutorial/title "The Area of a Rectangle"} :step/id #uuid "1a603e54-4f54-513f-82c5-b99d25dae778" :step/math-academy-id 9600 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106970}} {:db/id 17592186106970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105537 :question/id #uuid "cf89adb1-3344-5ed4-b2e0-48506af917bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-2940"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8e574a9-a37d-512f-aa4d-543ad1a3de84" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106408} {:db/id 17592186106415}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Rectangle From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "adc09c20-5a5a-5c4e-9d39-c6bae768710b" :step/math-academy-id 9601 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106973}} {:db/id 17592186106973 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105935 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105538 :question/id #uuid "022da369-7dfd-5865-8e72-4317203ad11e" :question/math-academy-id "e-2941"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0726a51-b1a9-5755-a19b-0cc68f96b875" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106416} {:db/id 17592186106417}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of a Side of a Rectangle Given Another Side and Its Area"} :step/id #uuid "405a478b-76e6-5357-a2ad-65d8bc8e55d8" :step/math-academy-id 9604 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106796}}] :activity/title "Areas of Rectangles and Squares" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105987} {:db/id 17592186106964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107049 :tutorial/content "The **area** of a shape is a measure of how much space is enclosed by a shape on a plane. Let's consider a square with sides of length of $1\,\textrm{in}$.

![](images/bc/bc59b6e5a60a2f22e6c7fb102eba2f255dd09e115fd04a16050570f9f8b053f4.png)

The area of this square is equal to ${\color{red}{1\,\textrm{in}^2}}$, which we say in words as "one square inch."

Similarly, if we have three squares with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$, $1\,\textrm{m}$, and $1\,\textrm{ft}$ respectively, then their respective areas will be
$1\,\textrm{cm}^2, \qquad 1\,\textrm{m}^2, \qquad 1\,\textrm{ft}^2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1b7b7096-09d8-55d7-a7bc-45c3a83c9412" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2302 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b19100e-d452-53e4-9fd7-da598e7cbf2e" :step/math-academy-id 9594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106965}} {:db/id 17592186106796 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105838 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105671 :question/id #uuid "08cf33de-c71e-55bb-8906-112075c06a37" :question/math-academy-id "e-7691"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "85c79564-93e7-5054-9534-71dc8dc54f7b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048360} {:db/id 17592186048921}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106186} {:db/id 17592186106187}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Rectangle or a Square Given Its Perimeter"} :step/id #uuid "470f5ea9-9e6d-525a-95cd-a5d8c2257844" :step/math-academy-id 28598} {:db/id 17592186107049 :tutorial/content "The **area** of a shape is a measure of how much space is enclosed by a shape on a plane. Notice that, this time, the sides of the square span multiple unit lengths.

![](images/14/1441893036f9a41ed0daa8c8ce078d6a733bab5bb88dc60259a6b9ebc1c2e7c0.png)

The length of one side of a grid square is equal to $1\,\textrm{cm}$. So, the area of one grid square is $1\,\textrm{cm}^2$.

Now, we need to find how many grid squares are contained inside $ABCD$.

![](images/5f/5f293762b05013689996298a7804fb5f507eb228112397641fb8f662ff74ba49.png)

Inside the large blue square, there are $3$ rows containing $3$ grid squares each, so we can fit exactly

$$
3 \times 3 = 3^2 = 9
$$

grid squares inside $ABCD$.

Each grid square has area $1\,\textrm{cm}^2$, so the area $\mathcal A$ of $ABCD$ is

$$
\mathcal{A} = (3\,\textrm{cm})^2 = 9\,\textrm{cm}^2
$$

In general, if we have a square with a side of length $a$, then the area of the square is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a^2
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5e28b50-44b1-59d2-a7d6-e3ffb7a10038" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2303 :tutorial/title "The Area of a Square"} :step/id #uuid "e7fe8167-acaa-551f-8d92-567afcc40716" :step/math-academy-id 9595 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106967}} {:db/id 17592186107050 :tutorial/content "Let's now suppose that we would like to compute the area of the square $ABCD$, shown below. :question/id #uuid "ed569da8-3409-5fe1-8ef1-066e28479e53" :question/math-academy-id "e-347" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100836 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44e6a31e-57dc-533f-972b-bdf2882f3e24" :knowledge-point/title "Maximizing the Area of a Circular Sector With a Fixed Perimeter"}] :question/problem "Suppose that we have a string of length $20$ inches and that we shape it to make a circular sector, as shown in the diagram below. Among all of the circular sectors that can be made with that string, what's the radius of the one that gives the largest area?

![](images/04/0473dd96f4f5f27c03d0ecbbba7ed0c0458527e71f515e242ec790d1dfea2d09.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ stand for the circular sector's radius and let $\theta$ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta
$$

We know that the perimeter of our sector is fixed at $20$ inches in length, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
20=2r + r\theta
$$

where we recall that $s=r\theta$ gives the arc-length $s$ of a circular sector of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$, where $\theta$ is in radians.

Now, by making $\theta$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that

$$
\theta = \dfrac{20-2r}{r} = \dfrac{20}{r} -2
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} A(r) &= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{20}{r} -2\right) \\[3pt] &= 10r -r^2. \end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A$, so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
A'(r) = 10 -2r
$$

Setting $A'(r) = 0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
A^{′}(r) &= 0 \\
10 - 2r &= 0 \\
r &= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=5$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
A''(r) = -2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad A''(5) = -2 < 0
$$

Since $A''(5)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=5$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r)$.

Therefore, the circular sector of the greatest area will have a radius of $5\,\textrm{in}$, and the maximum area is given by

$$
A(5) = 10(5) - 5^2 = 25\,\textrm{in}^2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048883} {:db/id 17592186049173} {:db/id 17592186050622} {:db/id 17592186101184 :question/id #uuid "22cfd715-0ade-5eef-b533-efccf1f8bf1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-15070"} {:db/id 17592186101473 :question/id #uuid "51226c54-f0bb-54ea-8fe1-5b6932a750bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-51212"} {:db/id 17592186100837 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100647 :question/id #uuid "be781400-b8ab-5673-952c-104306590d99" :question/math-academy-id "e-348"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bf444699-9f3f-5e1e-9ead-b9f2dabbdbb3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048322} {:db/id 17592186048921} {:db/id 17592186049179}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101185 :question/id #uuid "c2799bec-08ba-578d-938f-f2f2529b427d" :question/math-academy-id "q-15078"} {:db/id 17592186101259 :question/id #uuid "c53d7e6b-798c-5b95-b668-c7d8d0b22431" :question/math-academy-id "q-17946"}] :knowledge-point/title "Minimizing the Perimeter of a Circular Sector With a Fixed Area"} {:db/id 17592186100647 :question/id #uuid "be781400-b8ab-5673-952c-104306590d99" :question/math-academy-id "e-348" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100837 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bf444699-9f3f-5e1e-9ead-b9f2dabbdbb3" :knowledge-point/title "Minimizing the Perimeter of a Circular Sector With a Fixed Area"}] :question/problem "Consider all circular sectors $MON$ with area $A=8$ square units. What is the angle $\theta$ of the circular sector that has the smallest possible perimeter?

![](images/c8/c8b9506069c1b1d974399ad5afb751a79c9cced3e984cd5c38725d31a045aecd.png)" :question/worked-solution "We let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta$ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. Then, we want to minimize the perimeter

$$
P= 2r + r\theta
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $8$ square units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
8 = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta
$$

Now, by making $\theta$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned} 8 &= \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta \\[3pt] \theta &= \dfrac{16}{r^2}. \end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this value into our expression for $P$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= 2r + rθ \\
&= 2r + r \cdot \frac{16}{r^{2}} \\
&= 2r + \frac{16}{r}
\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P$, so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
P'(r) = 2 - \dfrac{16}{r^2}
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 - \frac{16}{r^{2}} &= 0 \\
2r^{2} &= 16 \\
r^{2} &= 8 \\
r &= 2\sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that

$$
r=2\sqrt{2}
$$

is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative

$$
P''(r) = \dfrac{32}{r^3} > 0
$$

, the stationary point

$$
r=2\sqrt{2}
$$

is a minimum.

Finally, when

$$
r=2\sqrt{2}
$$

, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ &= \frac{16}{r^{2}} \\
&= (16)/((2\sqrt{2})^{2}) \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the angle $\theta = 2$ radians minimizes the perimeter of the circular sector $MON$."} {:db/id 17592186048322} {:db/id 17592186049179} {:db/id 17592186101185 :question/id #uuid "c2799bec-08ba-578d-938f-f2f2529b427d" :question/math-academy-id "q-15078"} {:db/id 17592186101259 :question/id #uuid "c53d7e6b-798c-5b95-b668-c7d8d0b22431" :question/math-academy-id "q-17946"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186101621} :activity/id #uuid "004dc310-3a6e-5664-a905-c68173b8f37b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050620 :topic/id #uuid "59a5dc4d-5419-5445-ba51-b020f0d2e967" :topic/math-academy-id 1212} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102009 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to solve problems involving sectors of circles, such as finding the maximum area of the sector of a circle given a fixed perimeter. Let's remind ourselves of the general strategy for optimization problems.

1. Draw a diagram of the situation, introducing variables where necessary.
2. Write down the equation of the quantity that you're trying to maximize or minimize. This is called the **objective function**, and it might include more than one variable.
3. Write down the constraint equation.
4. Use the constraint equation to write the objective function in terms of a single variable only.

$\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1?$" :question/worked-solution "The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{R}$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1\right\}
$$

which can be written as

$$
\left\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{3^2} + \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{1^2} = 1\right\}.
$$

This is an ellipse centered at $(0,-1)$ with semi-axes of lengths $3$ and $1.$"} {:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186124828 :question/id #uuid $$
\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1,\,z=k
$$

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1}

[{:db/id 17592186125517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125830 :tutorial/content "A **cylinder** is a surface made by the set of lines that pass through a plane curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane and are perpendicular to this plane. The curve $C$ is called the **base curve**.

The familiar two-dimensional conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) can be used to describe cylinders. In this lesson, we'll explore these shapes.

An **elliptic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is an ellipse. If the ellipse lies in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of our elliptic cylinder is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse $C.$ In particular, if $a=b$, we get a **circular cylinder.**

**Watch out!** This may look like the equation of a regular ellipse. However, since we're now describing a surface in three-dimensional space, we assume that the $z$-coordinate is arbitrary. Thus, if we want $z$ to feature in our equations explicitly, we would write

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad z=k$$ where $k\in \mathbb R.$

For example, the graph of the elliptic cylinder

$$\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1$$

is shown below. The center of its base ellipse $C$ is at the origin, and the **axis** of the elliptic cylinder (the line through the center of the cylinder) is the $z$-axis.

![](images/50/504e609e134654d258378226d90f5faa8b9f6d12313a4fcac4a23d0bfe6bea52.png)

Let's describe some properties of this elliptic cylinder:

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1,$$ which is the base ellipse $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0)$ with semi-major and semi-minor axes of lengths $2$ and $1,$ respectively.

![](images/d0/d0e4c0630b0da60c4324330211ab1bf8090ebec067d9ebc2ac2a03056c500bd6.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to two lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/38/3813a5f43319056be03ddd8b3353ef3a8166b7495b32397c91066f40d0b33cd5.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to two lines in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/a0/a0d928060ad18d3ba677f5dd184777b833d3abf03226c04c21292e455bcd0518.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f8f004e2-d43f-5628-bbbe-4b3c7918a9f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4931 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "21ce271d-74a1-526d-a3bb-1e1dc0da83ed" :step/math-academy-id 30776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125519}} {:db/id 17592186125518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124587 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124398 :question/id #uuid "0cb849bd-8a9f-5305-b086-62da1a10e54f" :question/math-academy-id "e-8226"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36c5224a-eccc-5ea9-8719-2b0dc2ddb44d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186049477} {:db/id 17592186049699}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124828} {:db/id 17592186124892} {:db/id 17592186284487} {:db/id 17592186284488} {:db/id 17592186284489} {:db/id 17592186381313} {:db/id 17592186381320} {:db/id 17592186401488} {:db/id 17592186401495} {:db/id 17592186410158} {:db/id 17592186476898}] :knowledge-point/title "The Domain of a Cylinder"} :step/id #uuid "6b214232-840a-58b5-8946-bbbc69c878d7" :step/math-academy-id 30778 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125644}} {:db/id 17592186125519 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125831 :tutorial/content "A **parabolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a parabola.

If the parabola $C$ opens upward or downward when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by $$(x-x_0)^2 = 4p(y-y_0),$$ where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder $$x^2 = y$$ is shown below. Its base curve is an upward-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/03/03ab0a28802900d8076fdd5f555bdad6582c449441c46f1de74260013cc55119.png)

The trace of this parabolic cylinder can be either a parabola or a set of lines.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$x^2 = y,$$ which corresponds to the base parabola $C$ with its vertex at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/98/98124890d921c73d0cda54428ac803221d5f393384e14db2909b0138fda0fb93.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to a line in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{0}^{2} & =y \\ y & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to a line in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

On the other hand, if the base parabola $C$ is left-opening or right-opening when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by $$(y-y_0)^2 = 4p(x-x_0),$$ where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder $$y^2 = x$$ is shown below. Its base curve is a right-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

![](images/a8/a87267dbd77b1561c047c6228ba0c70b08e5a48228d7e0b6a161463045d5e22b.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4026d216-b14f-558d-a7a4-cf39aa550b45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4932 :tutorial/title "Parabolic Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "0e4c9032-faa3-5e93-a91c-a0a7db82838a" :step/math-academy-id 30779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125526}} {:db/id 17592186125520 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124588 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124399 :question/id #uuid "64fc4653-a2ba-5013-8c70-1f4f14e5f8be" :question/math-academy-id "e-8227"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abbeda26-2fc0-5195-be26-ae79c72fc7bf" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124878} {:db/id 17592186124879} {:db/id 17592186284480} {:db/id 17592186284481} {:db/id 17592186284484} {:db/id 17592186284485} {:db/id 17592186284486} {:db/id 17592186398597} {:db/id 17592186401467} {:db/id 17592186401474}] :knowledge-point/title "Traces of Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "595c41f8-1c2f-5e89-b663-e36a44f691ac" :step/math-academy-id 30781} {:db/id 17592186125526 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125834 :tutorial/content "A **hyperbolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a hyperbola.

If the hyperbola $C$ is horizontal in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by $$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,$$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder $$x^2 - y^2 = 1$$ is shown below. Its base curve is a horizontal hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/e3/e3c921cc7d6a1edbb182ecf158d7b84eb0d203fd20924d07cf57ca8f8ffdc107.png)

The trace of this surface can be either a hyperbola, a set of lines, or the empty set.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$x^2 - y^2 = 1,$$ which is the base hyperbola $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/19/19e02f27f625dd75d12333de3b82a7a012e4f6370c729eef5cd38a633c2c8689.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to a pair of lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/56/5679b53433493d8b6e92d5aa5273be30bbf67a9db51993a925423d8514571f05.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is the empty set.

On the other hand, if the base hyperbola $C$ is vertical when viewed from the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by $$\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} = 1,$$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder $$y^2 - x^2 = 1$$ is shown below. Its base curve is a vertical hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin, and the cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

![](images/d6/d690bca9515389bb403d0f205861af3294bc3a961df6691a5adb86de01421cff.png)

![](images/57/5763cb9b167c2e1e9d17c9778bf569a0efafb4fe36f97e05e8e2173fb29fc998.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "dba66b44-ad67-5d83-b191-e1d2f8b59ff8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7856 :tutorial/title "Hyperbolic Cylinders With Alternative Central Axes"} :step/id #uuid "85399770-a72b-521d-b90e-0e8d27d7e807" :step/math-academy-id 45326 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125520}}] :activity/title "Cylinders" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124698} {:db/id 17592186125517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125830 :tutorial/content "A **cylinder** is a surface made by the set of lines that pass through a plane curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane and are perpendicular to this plane. The curve $C$ is called the **base curve**.

The familiar two-dimensional conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) can be used to describe cylinders. In this lesson, we'll explore these shapes.

An **elliptic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is an ellipse. If the ellipse lies in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of our elliptic cylinder is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse $C.$ In particular, if $a=b$, we get a **circular cylinder.**

**Watch out!** This may look like the equation of a regular ellipse. However, since we're now describing a surface in three-dimensional space, we assume that the $z$-coordinate is arbitrary. Thus, if we want $z$ to feature in our equations explicitly, we would write

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad z=k$$ where $k\in \mathbb R.$

For example, the graph of the elliptic cylinder

$$\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1$$

is shown below. The center of its base ellipse $C$ is at the origin, and the **axis** of the elliptic cylinder (the line through the center of the cylinder) is the $z$-axis.

![](images/50/504e609e134654d258378226d90f5faa8b9f6d12313a4fcac4a23d0bfe6bea52.png)

Let's describe some properties of this elliptic cylinder:

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1,$$ which is the base ellipse $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0)$ with semi-major and semi-minor axes of lengths $2$ and $1,$ respectively.

![](images/d0/d0e4c0630b0da60c4324330211ab1bf8090ebec067d9ebc2ac2a03056c500bd6.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to two lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/38/3813a5f43319056be03ddd8b3353ef3a8166b7495b32397c91066f40d0b33cd5.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to two lines in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/a0/a0d928060ad18d3ba677f5dd184777b833d3abf03226c04c21292e455bcd0518.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f8f004e2-d43f-5628-bbbe-4b3c7918a9f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4931 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "21ce271d-74a1-526d-a3bb-1e1dc0da83ed" :step/math-academy-id 30776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125519}} {:db/id 17592186125830 :tutorial/content "A **cylinder** is a surface made by the set of lines that pass through a plane curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane and are perpendicular to this plane. If the parabola $C$ opens upward or downward when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by $$(x-x_0)^2 = 4p(y-y_0),$$ where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder $$x^2 = y$$ is shown below. Its base curve is an upward-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/03/03ab0a28802900d8076fdd5f555bdad6582c449441c46f1de74260013cc55119.png)

The trace of this parabolic cylinder can be either a parabola or a set of lines.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$x^2 = y,$$ which corresponds to the base parabola $C$ with its vertex at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/98/98124890d921c73d0cda54428ac803221d5f393384e14db2909b0138fda0fb93.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to a line in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{0}^{2} & =y \\ y & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to a line in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

On the other hand, if the base parabola $C$ is left-opening or right-opening when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by $$(y-y_0)^2 = 4p(x-x_0),$$ where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder $$y^2 = x$$ is shown below. Its base curve is a right-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

![](images/a8/a87267dbd77b1561c047c6228ba0c70b08e5a48228d7e0b6a161463045d5e22b.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4026d216-b14f-558d-a7a4-cf39aa550b45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4932 :tutorial/title "Parabolic Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "0e4c9032-faa3-5e93-a91c-a0a7db82838a" :step/math-academy-id 30779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125526}} {:db/id 17592186125518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124587 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124398 :question/id #uuid "0cb849bd-8a9f-5305-b086-62da1a10e54f" :question/math-academy-id "e-8226"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36c5224a-eccc-5ea9-8719-2b0dc2ddb44d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186049477} {:db/id 17592186049699}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124828} {:db/id 17592186124892} {:db/id 17592186284487} {:db/id 17592186284488} {:db/id 17592186284489} {:db/id 17592186381313} {:db/id 17592186381320} {:db/id 17592186401488} {:db/id 17592186401495} {:db/id 17592186410158} {:db/id 17592186476898}] :knowledge-point/title "The Domain of a Cylinder"} :step/id #uuid "6b214232-840a-58b5-8946-bbbc69c878d7" :step/math-academy-id 30778 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125644}} {:db/id 17592186125644 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125884 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered cylinders whose axes are parallel to the $z$-axis. - Consider the elliptic cylinder $C$ whose base curve lies in the $xz$-plane.

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1
$$

In this case, the axis of the elliptic cylinder is the $y$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/f3/f32db327a6e1f54d5b346af4ea2f9b0bcfce7f82c1b6e44375f398705acd4f63.png)

- Consider the elliptic cylinder $C$ whose base curve lies in the $yz$-plane.

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1
$$

"q-164424" :question/problem "What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1?$" :question/worked-solution "The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1}
$$

which can be written as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{{6}^{2}}=1}.
$$

This is an ellipse centered at $(4,2)$ with semi-axes of lengths $2$ and $6.$"} :step/id #uuid "33921a36-2e91-50fa-a06c-a30b1124550d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410159}} {:answer-field/choices However, since the equation has no (explicit) $y$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-3)^{2} & =12(z+1) \\ (x-3)^{2} & =3(z+1) \\ (x-3)^{2} & =4\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot (z+1).\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xz$-plane with the vertex at $(3,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid "5707a2b8-ff1e-50c1-9adc-a0aa60ce9a37" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410160}} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177028 :tutorial/content "Recall that Euler's number can be defined as the following special limit:

$$
e = \lim_{m \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{m}\right)^{m}
$$

We can derive an alternative version of this limit by making the substitution

$$
n=\dfrac 1m
$$

First, we note that if $m\to \infty$ then $n \to 0$. Therefore, applying our substitution, we arrive at the following important result:

$$
e = \lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+{n}\right)^{1/n}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "490157c8-33d8-5f0d-ad6e-f837c839499f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5709 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ef158b4c-de98-5033-958d-aa50b93d6909" :step/math-academy-id 35058 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176804}} {:db/id 17592186176794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176018 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175873 :question/id #uuid "1cc5d11a-c497-5d8f-84b4-9cbef561db28" :question/math-academy-id "e-9364"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9c8893eb-cc9c-59b1-98c8-ec326a352e28" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049769}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176301} {:db/id 17592186176308}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Limit Using the Alternative Limit Definition of Euler's Number"} :step/id #uuid "ac8ee34c-7875-5657-81c3-a58946bcf638" :step/math-academy-id 35060 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176796}} {:db/id 17592186176795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176019 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175874 :question/id #uuid "caad75a3-4ee4-5038-b9e1-5e296d83974a" :question/math-academy-id "e-9366"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6dbad5d4-6001-5be5-9ed3-0b959f4d7d92" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176300} {:db/id 17592186176302}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Limit Using a Variable Substitution"} :step/id #uuid "797a10b6-090b-55e9-8c36-939dfb954adc" :step/math-academy-id 35066 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176801}} {:db/id 17592186176796 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177029 :tutorial/content "Let's take stock of our two special limit definitions of Euler's number:

- $\displaystyle e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{n}$
- $\displaystyle e = \lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{1/n}$

We can use these results to evaluate more complex limits. For example, suppose we wish to evaluate the following limit:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right)^{x+3}}
$$

Notice that as $x \to \infty$,

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1$, while
- the exponent approaches $\infty$.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right)^{x+3}} = 1^\infty
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n = e
$$

In the given limit, we let

$$
\dfrac{2}{x+3}=\dfrac{1}{n}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{x + 3} &= \frac{1}{n} \\
x + 3 &= 2n
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$, we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → ∞)(1 + \frac{2}{x + 3})^{x + 3} &= lim_(n → ∞)(1 + \frac{1}{n})^{2n} \\
&= lim_(n → ∞)[(1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n}]^{2} \\
&= [lim_(n → ∞)(1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n}]^{2} \\
&= e^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "39210b04-2951-5b70-adbb-7a6690671dac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5710 :tutorial/title "Evaluating a Limit That Resembles a Special Limit Using a Variable Substitution"} :step/id #uuid "129e19b0-cbae-5677-bfcb-93c996ee597b" :step/math-academy-id 35067 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176795}} {:db/id 17592186176800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176022 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175877 :question/id #uuid "63c2e3b3-3418-5f74-8ebc-34af9fd6bf56" :question/math-academy-id "e-9377"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9308a83f-ed86-5cbc-9b23-c1fec9fca6a4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048515} {:db/id 17592186049226} {:db/id 17592186049442} {:db/id 17592186049760}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176299} {:db/id 17592186176307} {:db/id 17592186503687}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Limit Using a Variable Substitution: Advanced Cases"} :step/id #uuid "88bbb3ae-6920-5592-b9b2-5833516142b8" :step/math-academy-id 35109} {:db/id 17592186176801 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177032 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following limit:

$$
{\lim_{x \to 0} \left(1-\sin{x}\right)^{3/\sin{x}}}
$$

Notice that as $x \to 0$,

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1$, while
- the exponent approaches $\infty$.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} \left(1-\sin{x}\right)^{3/\sin{x}} = 1^{\infty}
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{1/n} = e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 0)(1 - \sin x)^{3/\sin x} &= lim_(x → 0)(1 + (-\sin x))^{3/\sin x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $-\sin{x}=n$. Therefore, since $n \to 0$ as $x \to 0$, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 0)(1 - \sin x)^{3/\sin x} &= lim_(x → 0)(1 + (-\sin x))^{3/\sin x} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{3/(-n)} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)[(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{-3} \\
&= [lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{-3} \\
&= e^{-3} \\
&= \frac{1}{e^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fdccc8f6-9726-5fd5-846c-74c2c5b1ed28" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5717 :tutorial/title "Evaluating a Limit Containing a Minus Sign Using a Variable Substitution"} :step/id #uuid "68a5d41c-4aef-5d14-b412-4042829e22c7" :step/math-academy-id 35113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176800}} {:db/id 17592186176804 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177035 :tutorial/content "We have shown that Euler's number $e$ is given by the following limit:

$$
e = \lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+{n}\right)^{1/n}
$$

Let's use this result to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{2/n}}
$$

Notice that as $n \to 0$,

- the exponent approaches $\infty$.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$

$$

which is an indeterminate form.

However, by rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and then applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{2/n} &= lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{2 \cdot 1/n} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)[(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{2} \\
&= [lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{2} \\
&= e^{2}

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "39210b04-2951-5b70-adbb-7a6690671dac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5710 :tutorial/title "Evaluating a Limit That Resembles a Special Limit Using a Variable Substitution"} {:db/id 17592186176800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176022 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175877 :question/id #uuid "63c2e3b3-3418-5f74-8ebc-34af9fd6bf56" :question/math-academy-id "e-9377"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9308a83f-ed86-5cbc-9b23-c1fec9fca6a4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048515} {:db/id 17592186049226} {:db/id 17592186049442} {:db/id 17592186049760}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176299} {:db/id 17592186176307} {:db/id 17592186503687}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Limit Using a Variable Substitution: Advanced Cases"} :step/id #uuid "88bbb3ae-6920-5592-b9b2-5833516142b8" :step/math-academy-id 35109} {:db/id 17592186177032 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following limit:

$$
{\lim_{x \to 0} \left(1-\sin{x}\right)^{3/\sin{x}}}
$$

Notice that as $x \to 0$,

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1$, while
- the exponent approaches $\infty$.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} \left(1-\sin{x}\right)^{3/\sin{x}} = 1^{\infty}
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{1/n} = e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 0)(1 - \sin x)^{3/\sin x} &= lim_(x → 0)(1 + (-\sin x))^{3/\sin x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $-\sin{x}=n$. Therefore, since $n \to 0$ as $x \to 0$, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 0)(1 - \sin x)^{3/\sin x} &= lim_(x → 0)(1 + (-\sin x))^{3/\sin x} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{3/(-n)} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)[(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{-3} \\
&= [lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{-3} \\
&= e^{-3} \\
&= \frac{1}{e^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fdccc8f6-9726-5fd5-846c-74c2c5b1ed28" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5717 :tutorial/title "Evaluating a Limit Containing a Minus Sign Using a Variable Substitution"} {:db/id 17592186177035 :tutorial/content "We have shown that Euler's number $e$ is given by the following limit:

$$
e = \lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+{n}\right)^{1/n}
$$

Let's use this result to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{2/n}}
$$

Notice that as $n \to 0$,

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1$, while
- the exponent approaches $\infty$.

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{\lim_{n \to 0} \left(1+n\right)^{2/n}} = 1^\infty
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

However, by rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and then applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{2/n} &= lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{2 \cdot 1/n} \\
&= lim_(n → 0)[(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{2} \\
&= [lim_(n → 0)(1 + n)^{1/n}]^{2} \\
&= e^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cde764e2-c036-59de-af59-f13454800e69" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5722 :tutorial/title "Evaluating a Limit Using the Alternative Limit Definition of Euler's Number"} {:db/id 17592186059869 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059460 :question/id #uuid "53dbcc31-f851-5f0f-84e8-ae06de2cc40b" :question/math-academy-id "e-2027"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1b701fb5-7676-5c5f-8a80-b86d2dec0548" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048263} {:db/id 17592186050625}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060048 :question/id #uuid "2c97ab89-6b99-583f-b8e1-78717190d044" :question/math-academy-id "q-1419"} {:db/id 17592186060312 :question/id #uuid "8ea4e5bf-c78f-5012-a71e-1e6ffea002af" :question/math-academy-id "q-61792"}] :knowledge-point/title "Creating an Exponential Decay Expression From a Decay Rate"} {:db/id 17592186059460 :question/id #uuid "53dbcc31-f851-5f0f-84e8-ae06de2cc40b" :question/math-academy-id "e-2027" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059869 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1b701fb5-7676-5c5f-8a80-b86d2dec0548" :knowledge-point/title "Creating an Exponential Decay Expression From a Decay Rate"}] :question/problem "Carlton initially made $\[math]40\,000$ annual profit from his business. [{:db/id 17592186060848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060871 :tutorial/content "A situation involves **exponential decay** if some initial amount repeatedly shrinks due to being multiplied by some constant rate.

For example, suppose that a certain battery had a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V}$ when it was healthy. Following a sharp impact, the battery's voltage decreased by

$$
\dfrac12
$$

every day since the day of the impact. What was the voltage of the battery $3$ days after it was damaged?

Starting with a voltage of $4\,\textrm{V}$, we know that this number will halve every day. So after $1$ day, the voltage (measured in volts) was

$$
{\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}
$$

On the second day, this number halved again. So the voltage after $2$ days was

$$
\left({\color{blue}{4\cdot \dfrac 1 2}}\right)\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}
$$

After one more day, the number above halves once again. So the voltage after $3$ days was

$$
{\color{red}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}}\cdot \dfrac 1 2 = {\color{black}{4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3}}
$$

If we evaluate the above expression, we get:

$$
4\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^3 = 4\cdot \dfrac 1 8 = \dfrac 1 2
$$

So after $3$ days, the voltage reduced to just

$$
\dfrac 1 2\,\textrm{V}
$$

This is an example of exponential decay. The voltage decreases by

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a time interval of $1$ day, every day. The voltage decays very rapidly, as we can see from the graph below.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Because $f$ is $8$-periodic on $[-4,4]$, we have $L=4$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231574 :question/id #uuid "0f970b89-f8e7-590f-9e3b-8ad7dbd8f9e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-343669"} {:db/id 17592186372872 :question/id #uuid 6722} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then

- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.

When $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$

Recall that for an equation of the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:

- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.

- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.

Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "67a0ca11-7450-5f6a-8bdc-4aee6301f209" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14775 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

Since the area of $\triangle CDE$ is $25\textrm{ cm}^2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 25 & =\frac{10\cdot CD}{2} \\ 25 & =5\cdot CD \\ CD & =5\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that $\overline{CD}$ is also the height of $\triangle ABC$ corresponding to the base $\overline{AB}.$

![](images/ea/ea7f44b91e87a42029c5f00aae97a2eebf2e472ff890d4b91f4973e1e383e5c7.png)

Therefore, we find the area of $\triangle ABC$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{AB\cdot CD}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 5}{2} \\  & =15{\text{ cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106155 :question/id #uuid "d8aab1ff-ffe9-5ce8-8bcd-5ec4903ad550" :question/math-academy-id "q-21030"} {:db/id 17592186106388 :question/id #uuid Quadric Surfaces by Completing the Square"}] :question/problem "Identify the surface $-x^2 + z^2 + 2x + y=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square in the $x$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2x+y & =0 \\ -({x}^{2}-2x)+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}-(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-y-1 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =y+1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1, -1, 0).$"} {:db/id 17592186124833 :question/id #uuid "acd3345e-478a-507e-b6c0-b18910d49c60" :question/math-academy-id "q-164554" $$
(x+2)^{2}=-y,\,-\infty <z<\infty 
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the equation of a parabolic cylinder, whose axis is the $z$-axis, is given by

$$
{x}^{2}=4py,
$$

and a parabolic cylinder, shifted ${x}_{0}$ along the x-axis and ${y}_{0}$ along the y-axis, is given by

$$
(x-{x}_{0})^{2}=4p(y-{y}_{0}).
$$

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(-2,0),\,p=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372321 :question/id #uuid "959722e2-9e2f-57fb-a069-bc3b5299d0b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-164471" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124651 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9840265f-02bf-58fa-94fd-77fb970af297" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Quadric Surfaces and Cylinders"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b4bb51d2-3c24-5582-8535-d4bcf0185cd1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "An elliptic cone" :db/id 17592186372323} {:answer/id #uuid "70c336ea-5c9f-53a0-81b3-3cc9b44928b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "An elliptic paraboloid" :db/id 17592186372324} {:answer/id #uuid "0db9e390-7be7-5570-9d97-7b82c83ea920" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "An elliptic cylinder" :db/id 17592186372325} {:answer/id #uuid "ccc499ec-42b9-5656-8096-e0e8e6657b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "A hyperbolic paraboloid" :db/id 17592186372326} {:answer/id #uuid "9c4c25b7-56dc-50c8-9b48-ed4ad3fab3c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "A hyperbolic cylinder" :db/id 17592186372327}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ccc499ec-42b9-5656-8096-e0e8e6657b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "A hyperbolic paraboloid" :db/id 17592186372326} :answer-field/id #uuid "798f1b60-69c5-522e-b6e6-b8a464f27287" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186372322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Identify the surface $z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-9{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $O$ is given by

| Surface | Equation | Image |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elliptic Cylinder | $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ | ![](images/2b/2b8788f027b93593a025542face33546425b057d1eb3b8e18da26e7774f6ed20.png) |
| Parabolic Cylinder | $x^2=4py$<br><br>$y^2=4px$ | ![](images/d3/d3f31aae01222e6a63e5de185c5b9f5a8af5aed8a750c6bc230e20e9fd93871a.png) |
| Hyperbolic Cylinder | $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$<br><br>$\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}=1$ | ![](images/15/159bb67600e079d9943ba6f79fcc6e580e3718f822dce50620c2bb6d2d9b76c8.png) |

Similar to quadric surfaces:

- We can generate cylinders with alternative orientation axes by describing a base curve in the $xz$-or $yz$-planes.

For example, the equation of an elliptic cylinder with its axis of symmetry along the $y$-axis is given by $$\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1.$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the equation of a parabolic cylinder whose axis is the $z$-axis is given by

Therefore, our equation is a parabolic cylinder whose axis is the $x$-axis and $p=-3.$"} :step/id #uuid "51825ebc-a150-59a7-947c-57e352dcf16a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406710}} {:db/id 17592186406710 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10cde161-28f6-55e5-986b-ad9855da614a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(-1,2,3)$" :db/id 17592186281844} {:answer/id #uuid "122b7f1a-d06c-5752-b881-d3aaf0a1f656" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1,-2,3)$" :db/id 17592186281863} {:answer/id #uuid "49873a52-1e06-5d10-9048-c31a56b3f6fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipsoid centered at $(1,2,-3)$" :db/id 17592186282313} {:answer/id #uuid "ca420948-0b66-53de-bd82-72e7dc4965ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1,2,-3)$" :db/id 17592186283457} {:answer/id #uuid "d9275452-1c1f-54aa-9f44-b0b79feef1b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An elliptic paraboloid centered at $(1,2,-3)$" :db/id 17592186283580}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283457} :answer-field/id #uuid "fd434c9b-d384-57dd-8332-85e7b5ec2000" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284382}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1b66372b-0da7-5bff-8ad5-ecdf16f5fac5" :question/math-academy-id "q-164549" :question/problem "Identify the surface ${y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x-4y-6z-4=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square in the $y$ and $z$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x-4y-6z-4 & =0 \\ ({y}^{2}-4y)-({z}^{2}+6z)-x-4 & =0 \\ (y-2)^{2}-4-(z+3)^{2}+9-x-4 & =0 \\ (y-2)^{2}-(z+3)^{2}+1-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-25{z}^{2}+16x+50z+91 & =0 \\ 4({x}^{2}+4x)+{y}^{2}-25({z}^{2}-2z)+91 & =0 \\ 4[(x+2)^{2}-4]+{y}^{2}-25[(z-1)^{2}-1]+91 & =0 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}-16+{y}^{2}-25(z-1)^{2}+25+91 & =0 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}-25(z-1)^{2}+100 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}-25(z-1)^{2}+100 & =0 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}-25(z-1)^{2} & =-100 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{100}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{4} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12x+8y-10 & =0 \\ 6({x}^{2}-2x)-4({y}^{2}-2y)-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6[(x-1)^{2}-1]-4[(y-1)^{2}-1]-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6(x-1)^{2}-6-4(y-1)^{2}+4-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6(x-1)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$6{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12x+8y-10=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square in the $x$ and $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12x+8y-10 & =0 \\ 6({x}^{2}-2x)-4({y}^{2}-2y)-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6[(x-1)^{2}-1]-4[(y-1)^{2}-1]-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6(x-1)^{2}-6-4(y-1)^{2}+4-6{z}^{2}-10 & =0 \\ 6(x-1)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}6(x-1)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2}-6{z}^{2}-12 & =0 \\ 6(x-1)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2}-6{z}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperboloid of two sheets centered at $(1,1,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "89ae8bd8-6821-50c2-ae85-b282e63cacb4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186499601}} {:db/id 17592186499601 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124831 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34a585bb-74c5-510e-a245-f4082f4c3979" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An elliptic cone whose axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis." :db/id 17592186282158} {:answer/id #uuid "44a458c1-9084-54b2-b8ff-98063908189d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperboloid of one sheet whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis" :db/id 17592186282270} {:answer/id #uuid "b1022887-6bfe-52a6-a0a8-8e1ab06354d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperboloid of two sheets whose axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis" :db/id 17592186283222} {:answer/id #uuid "b3c4e925-9bac-5dc9-a77e-70b58c292a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperboloid of two sheets whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis" :db/id 17592186283248} {:answer/id #uuid "cc208067-f320-5874-a23a-5da28c9ea960" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperboloid of one sheet whose axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis" :db/id 17592186283473}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283473} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3fd279c-bf2c-5eeb-b5e8-70142503f169" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284303}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a4c96dde-6df8-575b-bdd9-f49e9283853d" :question/math-academy-id "q-164373" :question/problem "Identify the surface ${z}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the equation of a hyperboloid of one sheet centered at $O$ whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis is given by

Using the graphical method, find the solution(s) of the following systems of equations:
${y =-x^{2} + 2; y =-2$" :question/worked-solution "The solutions $(x,y)$ of the system correspond to the intersection points of the two curves.

![](images/9f/9fe6da31061120bc2b654e64dedcfde1ca62beb2a96535031d302d11590747c1.png)

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=1-4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-3x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186478397 :question/id #uuid "46fed2b7-c806-57ef-a1e1-bd253db964cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-337443"} {:db/id 17592186478409 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y={e}^{-3x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =x{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049062} {:db/id 17592186050355} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1821fb92-1bc6-52cb-840b-fe52e847d9c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :topic/math-academy-id 2973} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186158408 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158527 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we’ll learn another method for solving inhomogeneous linear ODEs: **variation of parameters** (VOP).

Recall that a *first-order linear ODE* can be written in the standard form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} + P(x)y = Q(x).
$$

To solve it, we look for a solution of the form

$$
y(x) = y_c(x) + y_p(x),
$$

where $y_c(x)$ is the *complementary solution* (solution to the homogeneous equation) and $y_p(x)$ is a *particular solution* (any one solution to the original equation).

In variation of parameters, we start with the homogeneous solution and then allow its constant to vary with $x.$

- **Step 1:** Solve the corresponding homogeneous equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} + P(x)y = 0.
$$

Its general solution has the form

$$
y_c(x) = {\color{blue}C}e^{-\int P(x)\,\textrm d x},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

- **Step 2:** Guess the form of a particular solution by allowing the constant $C$ to depend on $x.$ 

We now choose an **ansatz**, meaning an *assumed form* for a solution. In VOP, we assume

$$
y_p(x) = {\color{blue}u(x)}e^{-\int P(x)\,\textrm d x},
$$

where $u(x)$ is an unknown function.

Intuitively, $y_p(x)$ has the same form as the homogeneous solution $y_c(x),$ but its amplitude changes with $x.$

- **Step 3:** Substitute $y_p(x)$ into the original ODE. 

Using the product rule, we find the derivative:

$$
y_p' = u' e^{-\int P\,\textrm d x} - u P e^{-\int P\,\textrm d x}.
$$

When substituted into $y' + Py = Q,$ the second term above cancels with $Py_p,$ leaving

$$
u'(x)e^{-\int P(x)\,\textrm d x} = Q(x).
$$

This allows us to solve for $u'(x),$ integrate to find $u(x),$ and finally recover $y_p(x).$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} + 3y = e^{2x}.

Let's solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution $y_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
y_c' + 3y_c = 0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c  = Ae^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable $y_p,$ we set $A = u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
y_p(x) = u(x)e^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of $y_p$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate $u'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{5x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{5x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $y_p = u(x)e^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5x}\cdot {e}^{-3x} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$
